ety.text: From Middle English cicle (“fixed length period of years”), from Late Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”), from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of chakra, chakram, charkha, chukker, cyclus, kike, and wheel (see there for more).
From -cycle (in bicycle, monocycle, and tricycle), perhaps associated with etymology 1. Compare French cycle in the same sense. The verb is either from the noun or a clipping of bicycle (verb).

senses.d: An interval of space or time in which one set of events or phenomena is completed.
ex: the cycle of the seasons, or of the year

senses.d: A complete rotation of anything.
A process that returns to its beginning and then repeats itself in the same sequence.
ex: electoral cycle    menstrual cycle    news cycle

senses.d: The members of the sequence formed by such a process.
A series of poems, songs or other works of art, typically longer than a trilogy.
ex: The Ring of the Nibelung is a cycle of four operas by Richard Wagner.

senses.d: A programme on a washing machine, dishwasher, or other such device.
ex: Put the washing in on a warm cycle.
the spin cycle

senses.d: A single, a double, a triple, and a home run hit by the same player in the same game.
ex: Jones hit for the cycle in the game.

senses.d: A closed walk or path, with or without repeated vertices allowed.
A chain whose boundary is zero.
An imaginary circle or orbit in the heavens; one of the celestial spheres.
ex: With centric and eccentric scribbled o'er, Cycle and epicycle, orb in orb

senses.d: To go through a cycle or to put through a cycle.
ex: When my wife and I heard a plaintive whinny from our laundry room the other day, we knew that our old dryer had cycled its last load.

senses.d: To turn power off and back on
ex: Avoid cycling the device unnecessarily.

senses.d: To maintain a team's possession of the puck in the offensive zone by handling and passing the puck in a loop from the boards near the goal up the side boards and passing to back to the boards near the goal
ex: They have their cycling game going tonight.

senses.d: A pedal-powered vehicle, such as a unicycle, bicycle, or tricycle, or a motorized vehicle that has either two or three wheels.
A bicycle.
To ride a bicycle or other cycle.
ex: I cycled the three miles each morning between hedges draped with spangled cobwebs and berried bryony.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French tor, from Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis).
From Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
Borrowed from Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”). Doublet of chakra.

Borrowed from Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”), from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of chacra.
Inherited from Middle French, from Late Latin cyclus.
From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).
Borrowed from English bike (verb).

Coined by English scientist and merchant captain Henry Piddington, probably in the 1840s, and based on some term in Ancient Greek. Sources disagree on the date and on which Ancient Greek term, though it had to be something derived from either κύκλος (kúklos, “circle, wheel”) or κυκλόω (kuklóō, “go around in a circle, form a circle, encircle”), for example the present active participle κυκλῶν (kuklôn). See cycle and wheel.

senses.d: Any weather phenomenon consisting of a system of winds rotating around a centre of low atmospheric pressure; a low pressure system.
ex: Near-synonym: storm

senses.d: A tropical cyclone occurring in the South Pacific or Indian Ocean.
ex: Near-synonyms: typhoon, hurricane

senses.d: The more or less violent, small-scale circulations such as tornadoes, waterspouts, and dust devils.
A strong wind.
A cyclone separator; the cylindrical vortex tube within such a separator
To separate using a cyclone separator.
To storm as a cyclone.
ex: What difference if it rained, hailed, blew, snowed, cycloned?

senses.d: To whirl in spirals as a result of a cyclone or whirlwind-like force.
ex: White dust was cycloning at the bottom of ravines that cut for miles into the red flatness
Pine needles cycloned wildly as Jan swung her car into the Institute's parking lot.

senses.d: To storm wildly; to be in a frenzy.
ex: The winds of change cycloned around Rhodesia and the debris began to fall within its borders.

grp.label: South Pacific and Indian Ocean weather phenomenon

ety.text: English cyclone.
From ciclo + -one.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κυκλῶν (kuklôn, “moving in a circle, whirling”), ultimately from κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
Borrowed from English cyclone, from Ancient Greek.
From cycle + -ist, 1882.

senses.d: A person who rides a cycle, especially a bicycle, or who habitually engages in cycling.
A motorcyclist.
ex: Most of the cyclists were members of the Pagans' Motorcycle Club of Washington.

ety.text: From cycle + -iste.
Calque of French cycliste.
Calque of French cycliste.

pt:ciclista.gl: biker; cyclist (a person who rides a bicycle)

senses.d: The activity of riding cycles, especially bicycles (for transport, sport, physical exercise, recreation, tourism...)
Bicycling.
The sport of riding and racing cycles, especially bicycles.
ex: In all my years as a cycling fan, I've never seen a breakaway like this.

senses.d: Any cyclic action or process.
ex: The cycling of the water softener in the basement was faintly audible from the kitchen.

senses.d: That undergoes a cyclic motion or process.
